newsitem.title: FRANCE: Earliest harvest in century for Bordeaux wines.
newsitem.headline: Earliest harvest in century for Bordeaux wines.

text.p: The Bordeaux wine harvest began on Monday more than a month earlier than usual, a once-in-a-century event that could yield 1997 vintage wines of exceptionally good quality, growers said on Monday.

Just a handful of white Bordeaux wine producers in the Pessac-Leognan region started picking their grapes, making it too early to say much about Bordeaux's more prestigious red wines, which will not be ready for harvest for another two weeks, during which the favourable weather could change.

Should the next two weeks remain hot and sunny, however, 1997 could be the third exceptional vintage in a row for red Bordeaux, which include such world-famous wines as Petrus, Lafite-Rothschild and Margaux and whose prices are already sky-high.

For the 1997 whites, "the quality already appears to be excellent," said Andre Lurton, the owner of Chateau Couhins-Lurton and Chateau Bonnet, who also is president of the Bordeaux Wine Trade Council.

"An advance in maturity can only help quality," Lurton told Reuters in a telephone interview. "The long days of summer have given the grapes long exposure to sunlight, leading to rich flavours, good levels of alcohol and acidity and excellent aromas."
Among other Pessac-Leognan chateaux which began harvesting on Monday were La Tour Martillac, Smith Haut Lafitte and Haut-Brion, Bordeaux growers said.
The earliest recorded harvest in this part of Bordeaux prior to this year was August 16, 1893, according to Jean-Bernard Delmas of Chateau Haut-Brion.
Over the last 100 years, the harvest typically has begun around September 20-25, he said in a statement.
"So 1997 is already a legendary vintage. With this exceptional precocity, there is no doubt that this wine will also be exceptional," Delmas said.
Lurton said the exceptionally early harvest was due to a combination of a mild winter, a springtime drought and lots of hot weather and sunshine during the summer months.
"We knew in April that the harvest would come before the end of August," he said. "But we haven't seen a harvest this early in 104 years."
Growers in other prestigious French wine-growing regions said their harvests also would be early although not as early as in Pessac-Leognan.

"The big question is whether the early harvest translates into quality," said Claire Contamine of the Burgundy Wine Board, who estimated that the Burgundy region was only about five to 10 days ahead of its normal harvest schedule, depending on the sub-region.
It was thus still too early to speculate on the vintage's quality, she said.
In the Champagne district, the harvest was also expected to take place early but not uniformly so, said Guillaume Bruneau of the Champagne Wine Trade Council.
The advantage of early maturity is that the grapes can be picked at their peak and under favourable weather conditions.

Rain is more common in September than in August, and harvest hopes can be dashed by heavy showers, which can dilute the flavour of the wine by diluting the juice in the grapes, or wet and clammy weather, which can rot the fruit, damaging flavours as well as harvest size.
